claims.source: We observed a significant induction of HbF in all the top eight target gRNA transduced cells in ABE (gRNAs- 2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, and -34), whereas only gRNA-2, -10, -11, and -42 expressed higher levels of HbF in CBE edited cells (Figure 3e–f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data shown in Figure 3e–f.

claims.claim: The increase in HbF variant is associated with compensatory downregulation of adult hemoglobin levels in the edited cells.
claims.source: Consistent with globin chain analysis, we observed that the increase in HbF variant is associated with compensatory downregulation of adult hemoglobin levels in the edited cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by HPLC data showing reciprocal changes in HbF and adult hemoglobin.

claims.claim: Among the validated top eight gRNAs in ABE and CBE, gRNA-2, -10, -11 with ABE and gRNA-2 with CBE resulted in a high target editing efficiency with a corresponding increase in HbF expression.
claims.source: Among the validated top eight gRNAs in ABE and CBE, gRNA-2, -10, -11 with ABE and gRNA-2 with CBE resulted in a high target editing efficiency with a corresponding increase in HbF expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of the relationship between editing efficiency and HbF expression across different gRNAs.

claims.claim: A high percentage of base substitution at the target site (more than 95%) was observed with ABE8e with the corresponding increase in the HbF positive cells and gamma-globin chains in both gRNA-03 and -11.
claims.source: We observed a high percentage of base substitution at the target site (more than 95%) with the corresponding increase in the HbF positive cells and gamma-globin chains in both the gRNAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a-c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a-c using ABE8e.

claims.claim: The frequency of larger deletions was significantly reduced with ABE8e perhaps because of the higher processive rate of ABE8e.
claims.source: The frequency of larger deletions was also significantly reduced perhaps because of the higher processive rate of ABE8e (Figure 3—figure supplement 4d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4d and inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Base editing at –114C > T, –115C > T and –116A > G mutations disrupts the binding of BCL11A and the base conversion at –198T > C and –199T > C affect the binding of LRF/ZBTB7A to the HBG promoter.
claims.source: Base editing of –114C > T, –115C > T and –116A > G mutations disrupts the binding of BCL11A and the base conversion at –198T > C and –199T > C affect the binding of LRF/ZBTB7A to the HBG promoter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about these mutations and their effects on transcription factor binding.

claims.claim: The installation of –113A > G and –198T > C mutations by gRNA-2 and gRNA-4, generate a binding site for GATA1 and KLF-1, respectively.
claims.source: Further, the installation of –113A > G and –198T > C mutations by gRNA-2 and gRNA-4, generate a binding site for GATA1 and KLF-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about these mutations creating transcription factor binding sites.

claims.claim: The base conversion at −175T > C by gRNA-3 (with ABE) creates a TAL1 binding site.
claims.source: Moreover, the base conversion at −175T > C by gRNA-3 (with ABE) creates a TAL1 binding site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about this mutation creating a TAL1 binding site.

claims.claim: The novel gamma-globin regulatory region identified includes the target base substitution mediated by gRNA-10, -11, -15, -21, -32, and -34 with ABE or CBE.
claims.source: The novel gamma-globin regulatory region identified includes the target base substitution mediated by gRNA-10, -11, -15, -21, -32, and -34 with ABE or CBE.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data identifying these novel regulatory regions.

claims.claim: With gRNAs -10 and -11, ABE converts nucleotide at –123T > C and –124T > C position, whereas CBE converts nucleotide at –122G > A (on-target editing site) and –117G > A (outside the editing window) positions.
claims.source: With gRNAs -10 and -11, ABE converts nucleotide at –123T > C and –124T > C position, whereas CBE converts nucleotide at –122G > A (on-target editing site) and –117G > A (outside the editing window) positions.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data showing the specific base conversions achieved by these gRNAs.

claims.claim: Target base substitutions at –123T > C and –124T > C positions result in greater induction of HBG expression, equivalent to that of the known HPFH mutations that disrupt the binding of BCL11A.
claims.source: Target base substitutions at –123T > C and –124T > C positions result in greater induction of HBG expression, equivalent to that of the known HPFH mutations that disrupt the binding of BCL11A.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction levels between the novel mutations and known BCL11A-disrupting mutations.

claims.claim: Electroporation of the ABE8e mRNA with gRNA targeting the BCL11A binding site (gRNA-2) and –123 novel cluster (gRNA-11) effectively generated highly efficient base editing at the target site in CD34+ HSPCs from healthy donor.
claims.source: Electroporation of the ABE8e mRNA with gRNA targeting the BCL11A binding site (gRNA-2) and –123 novel cluster (gRNA-11) effectively generated highly efficient base editing at the target site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from CD34+ HSPC editing experiments.

claims.claim: The editing efficiency observed at individual base positions were –110 (31%), –112 (37%), –113 (80%), and –116 (66%) with gRNA-2 and –123 (89%), –124 (91%) with gRNA-11 in CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: The editing efficiency observed at individual base positions were –110 (31%), –112 (37%), –113 (80%), and –116 (66%) with gRNA-2 and –123 (89%), –124 (91%) with gRNA-11 (Figure 4b).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequencing data shown in Figure 4b from CD34+ HSPC experiments.

claims.claim: The relative levels of HBG expression were significantly higher in gRNA-11 (>6-fold) and gRNA-2 (>5-fold) edited samples when compared to control (AAVS1 edited sample) by qRT-PCR in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: The relative levels of HBG expression were significantly higher in gRNA-11 (>6-fold) and gRNA-2 (>5-fold) edited samples when compared to control (AAVS1 edited sample) by qRT-PCR (Figure 4d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4d from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claims.claim: A significant downregulation of HBB and unchanged levels of HBA expression were observed in both the tested targets in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: In contrast, a significant downregulation of HBB and unchanged levels of HBA expression were observed in both the tested targets.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claims.claim: Flow cytometry and HPLC variant analysis confirmed the robust increase in the proportion of HbF positive cells and their HbF content compared with control samples for all the tested targets, with the higher effect in gRNA-11 in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: Flow cytometry and HPLC variant analysis confirmed the robust increase in the proportion of HbF positive cells and their HbF content compared with control samples for all the tested targets, with the higher effect in gRNA-11 (Figure 4e and g).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry and HPLC data shown in Figure 4e and g from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claims.claim: The globin chain analysis showed an increase in expression of HBG1 and HBG2 globin chain levels and a reduction of HBB globin chain level in erythroblasts derived from base edited CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: The globin chain analysis showed an increase in expression of HBG1 and HBG2 globin chain levels and a reduction of HBB globin chain level (Figure 4f).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RP-HPLC data shown in Figure 4f from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claims.claim: Base editing of the HBG proximal promoter with gRNA-2 or -11 did not alter enucleation potential or the expression of erythroid maturation markers CD235a or CD71 in erythroblasts derived from CD34+ HSPCs.
claims.source: Importantly, base editing of the HBG proximal promoter with gRNA-2 or -11 did not alter enucleation potential or the expression of erythroid maturation markers CD235a or CD71 (Figure 4h–i).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4h–i from CD34+ HSPC-derived erythroblasts.

claims.claim: A very minimal frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion was observed in CD34+ HSPCs electroporated with ABE8e and gRNA-2 or -11, which might be due to higher processivity and transient expression of the base editor mRNA.
claims.source: Finally, we determined the frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion in CD34+ HSPCs electroporated with ABE8e and gRNA-2 or -11. We observed a very minimal frequency of the 4.9 kb deletion which might be due to higher processivity and transient expression of the base editor mRNA (Figure 4c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4c and inference about the mechanism.

claims.claim: The level of HbF induction mediated by the installation of novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations (through gRNA-11) is comparable to the naturally occurring –115 cluster HPFH mutations (through gRNA-2) that disrupt the binding site of BCL11A.
claims.source: The present results suggest that the level of HbF induction mediated by the installation of novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations (through gRNA-11) is comparable to the naturally occurring –115 cluster HPFH mutations (through gRNA-2) that disrupt the binding site of BCL11A.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the experimental data comparing HbF induction levels in CD34+ HSPCs.

claims.claim: Adenine base editing of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoters to recreate the novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations is a potential approach for the therapeutic induction of fetal globin level and treatment for beta-hemoglobinopathies.
claims.source: Together, our data demonstrate that adenine base editing of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoters to recreate the novel –123 cluster HPFH-like mutations is a potential approach for the therapeutic induction of fetal globin level and treatment for beta-hemoglobinopathies.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from all the experimental data demonstrating therapeutic-level HbF induction.

claims.claim: The base editing at –123T > C and –124T > C sites by ABE creates the consensus binding site for the master erythroid transcription factor KLF1.
claims.source: Interestingly, we observed that the base editing at –123T > C and –124T > C sites by ABE with a single gRNA creates the consensus binding site for the master erythroid transcription factor KLF1 (Figure 5a and b; Tallack et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by sequence analysis and citation to Tallack et al., 2010 defining the KLF1 consensus binding site.

claims.claim: Modest but clear binding of KLF1 to the –123T > C and –124T > C mutated probe was observed in EMSA but not with the wild type probe.
claims.source: We observed modest but clear binding of KLF1 to the –123T > C and –124T > C mutated probe in EMSA but not with the wild type probe (Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b) or probes containing either –123T > C or –124T > C mutations alone (Figure 5c–d).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by EMSA data shown in Figure 5c–d and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b.

claims.claim: The combination of –123T > C and –124T > C mutation is important for the KLF1 binding to the HBG promoter.
claims.source: This confirms that the combination of –123T > C and –124T > C mutation is important for the KLF1 binding to the HBG promoter.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the EMSA data showing binding only with the double mutant.

claims.claim: A weak increase in the signal of KLF1 binding to the HBG promoters was observed in the cells edited to contain the –123 and –124 mutations by ChIP, but the effect was modest.
claims.source: We observed a weak increase in the signal of KLF1 binding to the HBG promoters in the cells edited to contain the –123 and –124 mutations, but the effect was modest, and a similarly weak enhancement was also observed at an arbitrary negative control locus, VEGF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c.

claims.claim: The KLF1 binding is at best weak and may be below the level of detection by ChIP.
claims.source: Thus, as seen in the EMSA, the KLF1 binding is at best weak and may be below the level of detection by ChIP.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from the weak ChIP signal.

claims.claim: Despite the higher on-target efficiency, off-target editing was not observed at the top target sites for gRNA-11 with ABE.
claims.source: Despite the higher on-target efficiency, off-target editing was not observed at the top target sites (Figure 6a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by NGS data of predicted off-target sites shown in Figure 6a.

claims.claim: The distribution frequency of A-to- I (in ABE) or C-to-U (in CBE) conversion across the base edited samples was very similar to that of the parental stable cell line.
claims.source: The distribution frequency of A-to- I (in ABE) or C-to-U (in CBE) conversion across the base edited samples was very similar to that of the parental stable cell line (Figure 6b–e).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 6b–e.

claims.claim: There is no significant difference between the edited and control cells except for both gamma- and delta-globin genes in differential gene expression analysis.
claims.source: We observed that there is no significant difference between the edited and control cells except for both gamma- and delta-globin genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by differential gene expression analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: ABE and CBE are useful in creating specific point mutations in the homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters, leading to a potential increase in the number of HbF positive cells and overall HbF production with a significant reduction in the larger deletion frequency.
claims.source: Overall, these results support that the ABE and CBE are useful in creating specific point mutations in the homologous HBG1 and HBG2 promoters, leading to a potential increase in the number of HbF positive cells and overall HbF production with a significant reduction in the larger deletion frequency.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by inference from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Current approaches to studying fetal globin regulation by programmable nucleases often result in the deletion of the HBG2 gene due to the introduction of DSBs in both HBG promoters.
claims.source: Current approaches to studying fetal globin regulation by programmable nucleases often result in the deletion of the HBG2 gene due to the introduction of DSBs in both HBG promoters (Traxler et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Traxler et al., 2016 documenting this limitation.

claims.claim: The elimination of the 4.9 kb intergenic region (including the HBG2 gene) appears to allow the locus control region (LCR) to directly interact with the HBG1 promoter and drive its expression.
claims.source: The elimination of the 4.9 kb intergenic region (including the HBG2 gene) appears to allow the locus control region (LCR) to directly interact with the HBG1 promoter and drive its expression (Métais et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Métais et al., 2019 describing this mechanism.

claims.claim: A base editing strategy converts target bases in the editing window without the generation of DSBs and hence largely avoids splicing of the HBG locus.
claims.source: A base editing strategy converts target bases in the editing window without the generation of DSBs and hence largely avoids splicing of the HBG locus.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by established knowledge about base editing mechanisms and data from the manuscript.

claims.claim: The larger deletions may be mainly a result of simultaneous CRISPR-Cas9-induced DSBs or by paired nickase-mediated two single-strand breaks (SSBs) on opposite DNA strands of the HBG1 and HBG2 gene.
claims.source: The larger deletions may be mainly a result of simultaneous CRISPR-Cas9-induced DSBs or by paired nickase-mediated two single-strand breaks (SSBs) on opposite DNA strands of the HBG1 and HBG2 gene (Ran et al., 2013a).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ran et al., 2013a and speculation about the mechanism of deletion formation.

claims.claim: Recent studies have shown the possibility of adjacent SSB on the same DNA strand leading to the formation of genomic deletions in plants.
claims.source: Interestingly, recent studies have shown the possibility of adjacent SSB on the same DNA strand leading to the formation of genomic deletions in plants. The deletion frequency depends upon the initial release of the single-stranded fragment between the two SSBs (Schiml et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Schiml et al., 2016 documenting this phenomenon in plants.

claims.claim: The conversion of the persistent nick into DSBs by the replication fork has been reported, where the R-loop primed replication fork encounters the single-strand nick site in DNA template and collapses to produce a DSB.
claims.source: Further reports suggest the conversion of the persistent nick into DSBs by the replication fork. The R-loop primed replication fork encounters the single-strand nick site in DNA template and collapses to produce a DSB (Kuzminov, 2001; Wimberly et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kuzminov, 2001 and Wimberly et al., 2013 describing this mechanism.

claims.claim: The concurrent introduction of SSB by base editors at the editing site of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoter might generate some 4.9 kb larger deletions, though very few were observed.
claims.source: Based on these findings, we predict the concurrent introduction of SSB by base editors at the editing site of the HBG1 and HBG2 promoter might generate some 4.9 kb larger deletions, though we observed very few.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the literature and the observed data.

claims.claim: Several different HPFH point mutations have been reported in the HBG promoters; and the effect of these mutations on gamma-globin expression in the native cellular environment has been deciphered for this limited set of mutations.
claims.source: Several different HPFH point mutations have been reported in the HBG promoters; and the effect of these mutations on gamma-globin expression in the native cellular environment has been deciphered for this limited set of mutations (Bauer and Orkin, 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Bauer and Orkin, 2012; Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2019; Wienert et al., 2017; Wienert et al., 2015) documenting known HPFH mutations.

claims.claim: Among the known HPFH point mutations, base conversion within the –115 cluster (from –110 to –116) showed the highest increase in promoter activity, confirming previous studies.
claims.source: Among the known HPFH point mutations, base conversion within the –115 cluster (from –110 to –116) showed the highest increase in promoter activity, confirming previous studies (Fucharoen et al., 1990; Gilman et al., 1988; Zertal-Zidani et al., 1999; Motum et al., 1994).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by data from the manuscript and citations to Fucharoen et al., 1990; Gilman et al., 1988; Zertal-Zidani et al., 1999; Motum et al., 1994.

claims.claim: CBE-mediated base conversion (C- to- T) at positions –114 and –115 resulted in a significantly greater induction of HbF than the multiple A-to-G nucleotide substitutions at −110, –112, −113, and –116 positions made by ABE.
claims.source: CBE-mediated base conversion (C- to- T) at positions –114 and –115 resulted in a significantly greater induction of HbF than the multiple A-to-G nucleotide substitutions at −110, –112, −113, and –116 positions made by ABE.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction between CBE and ABE at the –115 cluster.

claims.claim: The major HbF repressor BCL11A directly binds to the core TGACC motif located at – 114 to –118.
claims.source: Recently, it has been shown that the major HbF repressor BCL11A directly binds to the core TGACC motif located at – 114 to –118 (Liu et al., 2018; Martyn et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2018 and Martyn et al., 2018 documenting BCL11A binding.

claims.claim: Naturally occurring HPFH mutations at –117G > A, –114C > A, –114C > T, –114C > G, and Δ13bp disrupts binding of BCL11A to the promoter.
claims.source: Naturally occurring HPFH mutations at –117G > A, –114C > A, –114C > T, –114C > G, and Δ13bp disrupts binding of BCL11A to the promoter (Martyn et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martyn et al., 2018 documenting these mutations and their effects.

claims.claim: The –113A > G HPFH mutation within the –115 cluster creates a binding site for the master erythroid regulator GATA1 without disrupting the binding of BCL11A.
claims.source: The –113A > G HPFH mutation within the –115 cluster creates a binding site for the master erythroid regulator GATA1 without disrupting the binding of BCL11A (Martyn et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martyn et al., 2019 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claims.claim: ABE-mediated T-to-C substitution at position –198 of the HBG gene promoter has previously been shown to be associated with British HPFH and substantially elevates expression of HbF by creating a de novo binding site for the erythroid gene activator KLF1.
claims.source: ABE-mediated T-to-C substitution at position –198 of the HBG gene promoter has previously been shown to be associated with British HPFH and substantially elevates expression of HbF by creating a de novo binding site for the erythroid gene activator KLF1 (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Tate et al., 1986 and Wienert et al., 2017 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claims.claim: The –175T > C HPFH mutation has been shown to promote enhancer looping to the HBG promoter through recruitment of the activator TAL1.
claims.source: Another known HPFH mutation (–175T > C) has been shown to promote enhancer looping to the HBG promoter through recruitment of the activator TAL1 (Wienert et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wienert et al., 2015 documenting this mutation and its mechanism.

claims.claim: Novel substitutions at –69 (C -to- T), –70 (C- to- T), –122 (G -to -A), –123 (T -to- C), and –124 (T -to -C) of the HBG promoters were identified as potential new regulatory mutations that can elevate gamma-globin expression.
claims.source: In addition to the known mutations, we have identified novel substitutions at –69 (C -to- T), –70 (C- to- T), –122 (G -to -A), –123 (T -to- C), and –124 (T -to -C) of the HBG promoters as potential new regulatory mutations that can elevate gamma-globin expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data identifying these novel mutations.

claims.claim: The levels of gamma-globin expression resulting from these novel mutations were very similar to those of well-characterized, naturally occurring HPFH mutations.
claims.source: The levels of gamma-globin expression resulting from these mutations were very similar to those of well-characterized, naturally occurring HPFH mutations.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing HbF induction levels.

claims.claim: The observation that a de novo KLF1 site formed by the –198T-to-C mutation can upregulate fetal globin raises the possibility that introduction of a KLF1 binding site anywhere around the HBG promoter could potentially upregulate HBG gene expression.
claims.source: This result, together with the observation that a de novo KLF1 site formed by the –198T-to-C mutation can upregulate fetal globin (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017) raises the possibility that introduction of a KLF1 binding site anywhere around the HBG promoter could potentially upregulate HBG gene expression.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculation based on inference from the data and cited literature (Tate et al., 1986; Wienert et al., 2017).

claims.claim: The relative proximity of the –123/–124 site to the BCL11A site, that begins around –117, suggests it may also directly or indirectly affect BCL11A binding.
claims.source: The relative proximity of this site to the BCL11A site, that begins around –117, suggests it may also directly or indirectly affect BCL11A binding.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculation based on the proximity of the sites.

claims.claim: The availability of NGG PAM sequences in the target region confines the resolution of the screening approach.
claims.source: The availability of NGG PAM sequences in the target region confines the resolution of the screening approach.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about the limitations of PAM-dependent CRISPR systems.

claims.claim: The editing efficiency for ABE7.10 RA or BE3RA-FNLS is not uniform across the target regions.
claims.source: The editing efficiency for ABE7.10 RA or BE3RA-FNLS is not uniform across the target regions (Koblan et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Koblan et al., 2018 and data from the manuscript.

claims.claim: The current base editors are mainly involved in the installation of transition mutations, making the effect of transverse mutation in the target region on gene regulation not possible.
claims.source: The effect of transverse mutation in the target region on gene regulation is not possible as the current base editors are mainly involved in the installation of transition mutations (Gaudelli et al., 2017; Komor et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gaudelli et al., 2017 and Komor et al., 2016 describing base editor capabilities.

claims.claim: The bystander mutation introduced by the base editors at the target regions makes it difficult to identify functional regulatory single nucleotides responsible for the gamma-globin regulation.
claims.source: The bystander mutation introduced by the base editors at the target regions makes it difficult to identify functional regulatory single nucleotides responsible for the gamma-globin regulation.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on knowledge about base editor limitations and inference from the data.

claims.claim: The translational potential of genome edited HSPCs depends on long-term engraftment and repopulation ability.
claims.source: The translational potential of genome edited HSPCs depends on long-term engraftment and repopulation ability.
claims.evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about HSPC transplantation requirements.

claims.claim: Genotoxicity and cytotoxicity that can arise as a result of DSBs generated by programmable nucleases can be a limiting factor.
claims.source: However, genotoxicity and cytotoxicity that can arise as a result of DSBs generated by programmable nucleases can be a limiting factor (Cullot et al., 2019; Yu et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cullot et al., 2019 and Yu et al., 2016 documenting these concerns.

claims.claim: A previous study in nonhuman primates observed that the HBG promoter editing by Cas9 resulted in HBG2 deletion with up to 27% frequency and that cells with this deletion were under-represented after engraftment.
claims.source: A previous study in nonhuman primates observed that the HBG promoter editing by Cas9 resulted in HBG2 deletion with up to 27% frequency and that cells with this deletion were under-represented after engraftment (Humbert et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Humbert et al., 2019 documenting these findings in nonhuman primates.

claims.claim: Base editing at the target sites of HBG1 and HBG2 promoter by ABE and CBE does not result in high frequency of large deletions in the intergenic region as seen with Cas9 and only showed low levels of indel formation.
claims.source: Base editing at the target sites of HBG1 and HBG2 promoter by ABE and CBE does not result in high frequency of large deletions in the intergenic region as seen with Cas9 and only showed low levels of indel formation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing deletion frequencies between base editors and Cas9.

claims.claim: ABEs have an inherent advantage over CBEs as they generate desired edits (A:T to G:C) with high fidelity, whereas the latter generate unanticipated edits.
claims.source: ABEs have an inherent advantage over CBEs as they generate desired edits (A:T to G:C) with high fidelity, whereas the latter generate unanticipated edits.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing product purity between ABE and CBE.

claims.claim: ABE is a better base editor than CBE with respect to purity of base conversion and indel formation, in corroboration with existing findings.
claims.source: In corroboration with existing findings, our results also suggest that ABE is a better base editor than CBE with respect to purity of base conversion and indel formation (Lee et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claims.claim: The study did not observe any significant DNA and RNA off-target in the ABE and CBE edited cells.
claims.source: Further, our study did not observe any significant DNA and RNA off-target in the ABE and CBE edited cells.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by off-target analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: CRISPR base editing can be utilized to drive the expression of HbF to therapeutically relevant levels in an erythroid progenitor cell line and in HSPCs.
claims.source: In summary, we have demonstrated that CRISPR base editing can be utilized to drive the expression of HbF to therapeutically relevant levels in an erythroid progenitor cell line and in HSPCs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from HUDEP-2 cells and CD34+ HSPCs.

claims.claim: After screening every gRNAs within the 320 bp region of the HBG promoter, nine gRNAs were identified that, when paired with the appropriate base editor, can introduce HPFH-like mutations without the generation of indels.
claims.source: After screening every gRNAs within the 320 bp region of the HBG promoter, we identified nine gRNAs that, when paired with the appropriate base editor, can introduce HPFH-like mutations without the generation of indels.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Five novel regulatory regions for HBG1 and HBG2 that are required for the silencing of gamma-globin in adult erythroid cells were identified, shedding light on the molecular mechanisms behind hemoglobin switching.
claims.source: We identified five novel regulatory regions for HBG1 and HBG2 that are required for the silencing of gamma-globin in adult erythroid cells shedding light on the molecular mechanisms behind hemoglobin switching (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by the screening data and shown in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Base editing strategy will be among the pre-eminent therapeutic strategies for monogenetic disorders like beta-hemoglobinopathies in the future.
claims.source: Our work is an exemplification of base editors in mapping gene regulatory elements in highly homologous locus and we hope base editing strategy will be among the pre-eminent therapeutic strategies for monogenetic disorders like beta-hemoglobinopathies in the future.
claims.evidence: This claim is speculation about the future therapeutic potential of base editing.

results.result: Naturally occurring HPFH mutations in the HBG promoter increase fetal hemoglobin expression and ameliorate symptoms in patients with beta-hemoglobinopathies. HbF is normally silenced after birth to ~1% of total hemoglobin, but HPFH mutations reactivate gamma-globin expression, providing clinical benefit to patients with sickle cell disease or beta-thalassemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C4-C8 establish well-documented background knowledge about HPFH, HbF structure, developmental regulation, and clinical benefits. These claims are supported by multiple citations to established literature (Jacob and Raper 1958; Bauer and Orkin 2012; Thein 2018) and represent consensus scientific understanding in the field.

results.result: Known HPFH mutations create de novo binding sites for erythroid activators (TAL1, KLF1, GATA1) or disrupt binding sites for repressors (BCL11A, ZBTB7A/LRF). The –175T>C, –198T>C, and –113A>G mutations create activator binding sites, while mutations around –115 bp and –200 bp disrupt repressor binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C10, C35, C89-C96 describe well-characterized HPFH mutations and their molecular mechanisms, supported by extensive citations to prior work (Fischer and Nowock 1990; Martyn et al. 2018, 2019; Wienert et al. 2015, 2017; Liu et al. 2018). This represents established knowledge that provides context for the current study.

results.result: Nuclease-mediated approaches to introduce HPFH mutations have significant limitations, including inefficient homology-directed repair, high indel rates, and frequent 4.9 kb deletions between HBG1 and HBG2 genes due to simultaneous DSBs in the highly homologous promoters.
results.evaluation: Claims C11, C12, C82, C83 describe limitations of nuclease-based editing approaches, supported by citations to Cavazzana et al. 2017, Li et al. 2018, Métais et al. 2019, Wienert et al. 2017, and Traxler et al. 2016. This establishes the rationale for using base editing approaches.

results.result: Base editors (ABE and CBE) efficiently create point mutations in the HBG promoter with minimal indels and significantly fewer 4.9 kb deletions compared to Cas9. HUDEP-2 cells stably expressing ABE or CBE showed editing efficiencies of 10-51% (ABE) and 59-73% (CBE), with <2% indels and only 2-32% deletion frequency (ABE) or 0-12% (CBE) compared to 76% with Cas9.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C22 demonstrate the technical advantages of base editing over Cas9 for HBG promoter editing. The data show consistent editing efficiency, low indel rates, reduced deletion frequency, and preserved gene expression profiles (Figure 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1). The comparison to Cas9 is well-controlled and statistically significant.

results.result: A comprehensive screen of 41 gRNAs targeting the HBG proximal promoter (320 bp upstream of TSS) identified multiple regions that increase HbF expression. After excluding low-efficiency gRNAs, 30 ABE and 25 CBE gRNAs showed total editing efficiencies of 12-81% (ABE) and 13-80% (CBE), with HbF-positive cells ranging from 2-44% (ABE) and 1-35% (CBE). Five ABE gRNAs and one CBE gRNA showed >40% HbF-positive cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C34 describe a systematic screen of the HBG promoter region. The data are comprehensive, with editing efficiency measured by NGS and CRISPResso-2 analysis, and functional outcomes measured by flow cytometry (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1-3). ABE showed higher product purity than CBE, consistent with prior literature. The K562 control experiments appropriately test for disruption of activator binding sites.

results.result: Validation of the top eight gRNAs from the screen confirmed high editing efficiency (24-78% ABE, 36-85% CBE) with individual base conversions of 0-65% (A-to-G) and 1-57% (C-to-T), <2% indels, and equal editing efficiency between HBG1 and HBG2 promoters. Five gRNAs (gRNA-2, -10, -11, -32, -34) were effective with both ABE and CBE.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C42 validate the screening results with detailed characterization of editing patterns. The data show consistent editing between HBG1 and HBG2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-d), appropriate bystander editing patterns, and low indel frequencies. The phasing analysis using SNVs to distinguish HBG1 and HBG2 is methodologically sound.

results.result: Base editing with top gRNAs significantly increased HBG mRNA expression (p<0.01-0.0001 for all ABE gRNAs; p<0.05-0.0001 for CBE gRNAs-2, -10, -11, -42) and gamma-globin chain levels (10-30% of beta-like globin for ABE; 6-45% for CBE) without affecting erythroid differentiation. The 4.9 kb deletion frequency was 2-32% (ABE) and 0-12% (CBE), with high correlation (r=0.71) between deletion frequency and reduced HBG2 expression in ABE samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C51 demonstrate functional consequences of base editing with appropriate molecular and cellular assays (qRT-PCR, RP-HPLC, flow cytometry). The reciprocal changes in gamma- and beta-globin chains maintain the alpha/beta-like ratio. The correlation analysis appropriately distinguishes deletion-dependent (ABE) from deletion-independent (CBE) mechanisms of reduced HBG2 expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).

results.result: HPLC analysis confirmed significant HbF induction in all eight ABE-edited samples (gRNAs-2, -3, -4, -10, -11, -15, -32, -34) and four CBE-edited samples (gRNAs-2, -10, -11, -42), with compensatory downregulation of adult hemoglobin. The hyperactive ABE8e variant achieved >95% base substitution with increased HbF levels and significantly reduced deletion frequency.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C56 demonstrate functional HbF production at the protein level using HPLC. The ABE8e data (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) show that improved editing efficiency correlates with better outcomes and fewer deletions, supporting the hypothesis that higher processivity reduces deletion formation. The relationship between editing efficiency and HbF expression is appropriately analyzed by PCA (Figure 3i).

results.result: The screen identified novel regulatory regions including the –123 cluster, where ABE-mediated –123T>C and –124T>C mutations induced HbF expression equivalent to known BCL11A-disrupting mutations. Known mutations (gRNAs-2, -3, -4) disrupt BCL11A/LRF binding or create GATA1/KLF1/TAL1 binding sites, while novel mutations (gRNAs-10, -11, -15, -21, -32, -34) identify previously unknown regulatory elements.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C62 identify novel regulatory regions while confirming known HPFH mutations. The comparison between novel –123/–124 mutations and known BCL11A-disrupting mutations is well-supported by multiple functional assays. The identification of five novel regulatory regions represents a significant advance in understanding HBG regulation.

results.result: Base editing of CD34+ HSPCs from healthy donors with ABE8e mRNA and gRNA-11 (–123 cluster) or gRNA-2 (BCL11A site) achieved high editing efficiency (89-91% at –123/–124; 66-80% at –113/–116) and induced >5-6 fold increase in HBG expression with robust HbF production, without affecting erythroid differentiation or enucleation. The –123 cluster mutations showed comparable or higher HbF induction than BCL11A-disrupting mutations, with minimal 4.9 kb deletions.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C72 demonstrate therapeutic potential in clinically relevant CD34+ HSPCs. The data include comprehensive characterization: editing efficiency (Figure 4b), gene expression (Figure 4d), protein levels (Figure 4e-g), differentiation markers (Figure 4h-i), and deletion frequency (Figure 4c). The use of transient mRNA delivery and ABE8e variant minimizes deletions. This represents strong proof-of-concept for therapeutic application.

results.result: The –123T>C and –124T>C mutations create a consensus KLF1 binding site. EMSA demonstrated modest but clear KLF1 binding to the double mutant probe but not to wild-type or single mutant probes. ChIP-qPCR showed weak KLF1 enrichment at the edited HBG promoter, suggesting KLF1 binding may be weak and near the detection limit.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C77 propose KLF1 binding as the mechanism for –123/–124 mutations. While EMSA clearly shows binding to the double mutant (Figure 5c-d, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a-b), the ChIP signal is weak and not significantly different from a negative control locus (VEGF) (Figure 5—figure supplement 1c). The authors appropriately acknowledge this limitation and note that alternative mechanisms (other activators, indirect BCL11A effects) are possible. Additional experiments are needed to definitively establish the mechanism.

results.result: Off-target analysis showed no DNA off-target editing at predicted sites for gRNA-11 with ABE. Transcriptome-wide RNA sequencing showed similar A-to-I (ABE) and C-to-U (CBE) conversion frequencies in edited and control cells, with no significant differential gene expression except for gamma- and delta-globin genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C81, C111 demonstrate specificity of base editing. DNA off-target analysis by NGS at 11 predicted sites showed no editing (Figure 6a). RNA-seq analysis showed no increase in transcriptome-wide deamination (Figure 6b-e) and no off-target gene expression changes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1). These data support the safety profile of the approach.

results.result: Base editing avoids DSBs and largely prevents large deletions, though some 4.9 kb deletions still occur. The deletions may result from concurrent single-strand breaks (SSBs) at HBG1 and HBG2 promoters, conversion of persistent nicks to DSBs by replication forks, or adjacent SSBs on the same strand, as reported in plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C88 propose mechanisms for residual deletions with base editors. While the observation of reduced but non-zero deletions is well-supported by data (C17-C18, C49-C51), the mechanistic explanations are speculative, based on literature from other systems (Ran et al. 2013a; Schiml et al. 2016; Kuzminov 2001; Wimberly et al. 2013). The variable deletion rates across gRNAs and between ABE/CBE suggest multiple factors, but direct experimental evidence for the proposed mechanisms is lacking.

results.result: The screen identified five novel regulatory regions (–69, –70, –122, –123, –124) and nine gRNAs that introduce HPFH-like mutations without generating indels. The novel mutations induced gamma-globin expression levels similar to well-characterized naturally occurring HPFH mutations.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98, C113-C114 summarize the key discoveries from the screen. The identification of novel regulatory regions is well-supported by the comprehensive screening data (Figure 2-3), functional validation (Figure 3-4), and comparison to known HPFH mutations. The claim of five novel regulatory regions is clearly documented in Figure 7.

results.result: The observation that KLF1 binding sites at different positions (–198, –123/–124) can upregulate HBG suggests that introducing KLF1 binding sites anywhere around the HBG promoter could potentially upregulate expression. The proximity of the –123/–124 site to the BCL11A site (–117) suggests it may also affect BCL11A binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 are speculative hypotheses about mechanisms and general principles. While the data support that multiple KLF1 sites can activate HBG, the generalization that KLF1 sites 'anywhere' would work is not tested. The suggestion about BCL11A binding is reasonable given proximity but lacks experimental support. These represent interesting hypotheses for future work rather than established findings.

results.result: The screening approach has technical limitations including: PAM sequence availability constraining resolution, non-uniform editing efficiency across target regions, inability to test transversion mutations with current base editors, and bystander mutations complicating identification of functional single nucleotides.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the approach. These are well-recognized constraints of base editing technology (supported by citations to Koblan et al. 2018; Gaudelli et al. 2017; Komor et al. 2016) and are honestly discussed. The authors suggest appropriate solutions including alternative PAM variants, hyperactive editors, dual base editors, and prime editing.

results.result: Base editing offers advantages over Cas9 for therapeutic applications in HSPCs. While Cas9 editing causes genotoxicity/cytotoxicity from DSBs and results in HBG2 deletions that are under-represented after engraftment (27% deletion frequency in nonhuman primates), base editing shows low indel formation and reduced deletion frequency. ABE has inherent advantages over CBE in product purity and indel formation.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C110 discuss translational implications, supported by citation to Humbert et al. 2019 for nonhuman primate data and Lee et al. 2018 for ABE/CBE comparison. The data from this study (C108-C110) support the advantages of base editing, particularly ABE, for therapeutic applications. However, long-term engraftment studies in animal models would strengthen these claims.

results.result: CRISPR base editing can drive HbF expression to therapeutically relevant levels in erythroid progenitor cells and HSPCs, and may become a pre-eminent therapeutic strategy for monogenetic disorders like beta-hemoglobinopathies.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is well-supported by the comprehensive data in HUDEP-2 cells and CD34+ HSPCs showing therapeutically relevant HbF levels (>5-6 fold increase, 10-45% of beta-like globin). Claim C115 is speculative about future therapeutic applications but is reasonable given the proof-of-concept data. However, clinical translation requires additional validation including long-term engraftment studies, in vivo efficacy in disease models, and safety assessments.

results.result: CBE-mediated base conversion at positions –114 and –115 resulted in significantly greater HbF induction than multiple A-to-G substitutions at –110, –112, –113, and –116 positions made by ABE at the –115 cluster.
results.evaluation: Claim C91 compares CBE and ABE editing at the –115 cluster (BCL11A binding site). The data show that CBE editing at –114/–115 (which directly disrupts the core BCL11A binding motif) is more effective than ABE editing at surrounding positions. This is consistent with the known importance of the –114/–115 positions for BCL11A binding (Martyn et al. 2018; Liu et al. 2018).
